choice_a: Reaching a conclusion that goes further than the text's clues support, often by adding outside knowledge.
feedback_a: Correct. Over-inference happens when the reader stretches the clues too far or imports outside knowledge.
feedback_b: Inference itself is good — over-inference is going too far.
feedback_d: Different skill — fact vs opinion isn't the same as inference vs over-inference.

prompt: What's the BEST test for whether an inference is over-inference?
choice_b: It's the SMALLEST conclusion the clue supports — anything bigger or more specific is usually over-inference.
feedback_b: Correct. The smallest, closest-to-the-clue conclusion is usually the defensible inference. Bigger conclusions need bigger clues.
feedback_d: Drama goes the wrong direction — the smallest claim is usually right.

prompt: Text: "Mia is a fifth grader who loves to read." Which of these is OVER-inference?
choice_a: Mia gets straight A's in school.
choice_d: Mia has probably read more than one thing.
feedback_a: Correct. Loving to read does not prove anything about grades. That conclusion imports outside assumptions.
feedback_b: This is a reasonable restatement of "loves to read."
feedback_c: This is directly stated, not an inference.
feedback_d: This is a small, reasonable inference from loving to read.

prompt: Text: "He frowned at the menu and ordered water." Which is OVER-inference?
choice_a: He didn't see something he wanted on the menu.
choice_b: His family is bankrupt and he's about to drop out of school.
choice_c: He may not have been hungry or may have been saving money.
feedback_b: Correct. The clue (frown + water) doesn't support a whole life crisis. The reader stretched a small clue into a big story.
feedback_c: Defensible — multiple small possibilities the clue could support.

prompt: Text: "The grandmother smiled when she saw the photograph." Which is the SAFEST inference (least over-inferred)?
choice_a: The grandmother is sad about her past.
choice_b: The grandmother regrets something in the photo.
choice_c: The photograph means something to her.
choice_d: The grandmother is going to throw away the photograph.
feedback_b: Doesn't support "regret" either — that's over-reading the smile.
feedback_c: Correct. The smallest, closest-to-the-clue inference. Why it matters isn't specified yet — that would be over-inference.

prompt: Text: "Tom didn't come to school for three days." Which is the SAFEST inference?
choice_a: Something kept Tom from school — possibly illness, possibly something else.
choice_b: Tom is in serious trouble at home.
choice_c: Tom's parents don't care about education.
feedback_a: Correct. Closest to the clue. Three absences without more context allows for many possibilities — name the range, don't pick one.
feedback_b: Over-inference — three days doesn't support a serious-trouble conclusion.
feedback_d: Adds an emotion the clue doesn't support.

prompt: A student thinks: "In real life, when a parent says 'we'll see,' they usually mean no. So in this story, when the dad says 'we'll see,' he probably means no." What's the problem?
choice_a: The student should infer something happier.
choice_b: The student is using outside knowledge ("in real life") instead of clues from THIS text. The story might use "we'll see" differently.
choice_c: The student's vocabulary is too small.
feedback_a: The conclusion's tone isn't the issue.
feedback_b: Correct. "In real life" is the outside-knowledge signal. The student should look for clues IN THIS text to support whether dad means no — not import a generalization.

prompt: Which is the BEST description of "staying inside the text"?
choice_a: Reading the text more than once.
choice_b: Quoting the text exactly in your answer.
choice_c: Reaching inferences only from the clues the text actually gives you — not from outside knowledge or speculation.
feedback_a: Rereading can help but isn't the definition.
feedback_b: Quoting is the move for evidence, not inference.
feedback_c: Correct. Inference works inside the text. Outside knowledge and speculation push you past what the clues support.
feedback_d: Other reading is fine — but during a question, work from THIS text.

prompt: Read: "Sara left her notebook on her desk before going home." Which is OVER-inference?
choice_a: Sara had a notebook at school.
choice_b: Sara may expect to return to that desk later.
choice_c: Sara's desk is in a school.
choice_d: Sara is failing all her classes and has given up on schoolwork.
feedback_b: This is a small, cautious inference from leaving the notebook on the desk. It does not invent a larger story.
feedback_d: Correct. Leaving a notebook on a desk doesn't support "failing all classes and given up." Massive over-inference from a small clue.

prompt: Which signal in a wrong-answer choice should make you suspect OVER-inference?
choice_c: It is shorter than the question.
choice_d: It claims something dramatic or specific that goes further than the text's clues — "His whole future is at stake," "She will never recover," etc.
feedback_d: Correct. Big dramatic claims need big text support. If the text only gave you a small clue, an answer claiming "whole future," "never," "forever," or similar is usually over-inference.
